roles.label: Service
roles.test: Deployed, started and stopped as a unit, with a runtime of its own; it answers requests or does work on its own schedule
roles.basis: The application container of the C4 model (C153) and the process of the data flow diagram in Microsoft's SDL threat-modeling article (C147); the service-dynamics rows are written about these.

roles.label: Datastore
roles.test: Holds state at rest that other elements read or write; does nothing on its own
roles.basis: The data-store container of the C4 model (C153) and the data store in Microsoft's SDL threat-modeling article (C147); the data items of the NASA Software Safety Guidebook (C137) are a basis for per-kind data fault types.

roles.label: Event stream
roles.test: Decouples producers from consumers in time: one queue, topic or log, never the broker
roles.basis: Queues and topics as containers in the C4 model (C154); the software events of the NASA Software Safety Guidebook (C138) are a basis for per-kind event fault types.

roles.label: Interface
roles.test: A contract between two elements that is analysed in its own right: its schema, versions, limits and error contract
roles.basis: The interface failure class of the NASA Software Safety Guidebook (C136) and the TSF interfaces of Common Criteria (C158).

roles.label: Component
roles.test: Everything else: code that ships inside another element's deployable and has no runtime of its own, including a library, a module, a handler, a job function, an ML model
roles.basis: The component of the C4 model (C153); the CSCIs, units, objects and instances a software FMEA inventories by design phase in the NASA Software Engineering Handbook (C135) are a basis for this role.

boundaries.label: In scope
boundaries.test: This analysis covers it: its sources are the repository, documents, incidents or people of the analysed system
boundaries.basis: The line between in scope and outside it rests on the scope of the analysed workload in the Azure Well-Architected Framework (C143) and in the AWS Well-Architected reliability pillar (C146), on the external systems the analysed system needs in MIL-STD-1629A (C134), and on the interactors outside the scope in Microsoft's SDL threat-modeling article (C149).

boundaries.label: Owned outside
boundaries.test: The organisation can change it, but this analysis does not cover it: another team's service, the deploy pipeline when not analysed, a shared library owned elsewhere
boundaries.basis: The split of the outside into owned outside and third party is the skill's own: no source draws it.

boundaries.label: Third party
boundaries.basis: The split of the outside into owned outside and third party is the skill's own: no source draws it.

security.label: Security-relevant
security.test: If this element misbehaves, can someone see or do what the system must prevent?
security.basis: The security-relevant components of NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 (C157), the TOE security functionality of Common Criteria (C158), and the isolation of security functions in NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 (C156), the reason the class is worth marking; the list of properties, authentication, authorisation, confidentiality or integrity, is the skill's own.

tie_breaks.text: A cache is a `datastore`. A broker is a `service`; its topics are `event_stream`s.
A third-party API: the provider is a `service` with `boundary: third_party`; its contract becomes an `interface` element only when the contract itself is analysed.
A platform you cannot decompose (a serverless platform, a cloud region) takes `service`; what it exposes and you depend on, such as a cache API, can be its own element with the fitting role.
Code that runs on the user's device but ships inside another element's deployable, such as a browser app served by its worker, is a `component` of that element.
A managed database or queue is `datastore` or `event_stream` with `boundary: third_party`.
An ML or LLM model is a `component` when it runs inside a service and a `service` when it is served separately.
Code that reads or writes a cache is a component of its element; the cache itself is the datastore.
A parent is judged on its own behaviour: a security flag propagates neither up to a parent nor down to a child.
An element outside the scope takes the security test like any other; a third-party identity provider, or a platform that holds the system's secrets, is security-relevant.
An item named as an API, endpoint or contract, with no deployable of its own named, is an interface.
